title: One month after the floods, efforts to restore education are helping children return to learning in Nepal - Unicef
description: One month after the floods, efforts to restore education are helping children return to learning in Nepal  Unicef
publisher.title: Unicef
full_article:
KATHMANDU, 23 September 2026 – One month after devastating floods struck central and northern Nepal, thousands of children continue to face disruptions to their education, highlighting the urgent need for sustained support to help them return to safe learning environments.

Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centres in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts. The disaster also had a devastating human toll, with around 440 students and education personnel reported dead or missing, including 414 children.

"Education is a critical part of children's recovery after a disaster," said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. "Returning to learning provides children with a sense of stability, routine and hope at a time when many have experienced significant loss and uncertainty."

Since the onset of the emergency, UNICEF has worked with the Government of Nepal and partners to help children resume learning as quickly as possible. To date, UNICEF has supported the establishment of 48 temporary learning centres, helping more than 1,400 children in flood-affected areas return to learning. UNICEF has also provided essential learning materials and psychosocial support to help children recover and continue their education.

While these efforts are helping children return to learning, recovery needs remain substantial. The Education Rapid Needs Assessment estimates that significant investment will be required to restore damaged education infrastructure and ensure children can continue their education uninterrupted.

UNICEF is calling for continued support for both immediate recovery efforts and longer-term resilience building, ensuring that every child affected by the floods can learn, recover and thrive. As Nepal moves from emergency response to recovery, there is also an opportunity to strengthen the resilience of schools, health facilities, water and sanitation systems, and other critical infrastructure to better withstand future shocks. With climate-related disasters becoming more frequent and severe, investments in climate-resilient infrastructure, preparedness and social services are critical to help protect children and communities from future disruptions.

"When floods damage schools, children don't just lose classrooms. We miss lessons, fall behind in our studies, spend less time with our friends and teachers, and lose the routines that help us feel safe and supported," said Jayanti Bam, UNICEF Nepal's Youth Advocate for Climate Action. "We need stronger schools that can withstand disasters. We also need to know what to do when there is a flood, landslide, or other emergency. And if our schools are damaged, we need ways to keep learning, whether in a temporary learning space or online, so our education can continue."

One month after the floods, thousands of children and their families are still enduring the consequences every day. Many families remaindisplaced, some schools are still being used as temporary shelters, and damaged roads and bridges continue to limit access to critical education, health, water and sanitation services in some of the hardest-hit communities.

full_article:
US Pledges $31 Million for Nepal Flood Relief, Recovery

WASHINGTON, DC- The United States announced plans to provide an additional $31 million to support Nepal’s recovery from devastating floods, including funding for permanent bridges, humanitarian assistance and drones manufactured in the US.

The announcement came as about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following the disaster.

US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker announced the proposed assistance during a meeting with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal in New York, according to the US State Department.

Hooker conveyed US sympathies to those affected by the floods, including families of Americans whose whereabouts remained unknown.

The largest component of the package is $13 million for US-manufactured drones intended to strengthen Nepal’s ability to respond to future disasters and support recovery operations.

The State Department did not provide details about the type or number of drones under consideration or identify the US manufacturers that could supply them.

Washington also plans to work with Congress to provide $10 million for permanent, custom-built bridges. The bridges will be sourced from an American company, the department said.

The proposed bridges are intended to restore transport links damaged by the flooding and improve regional connectivity in affected areas. Roads and bridges are particularly important in Nepal, where difficult mountain terrain can leave communities isolated after floods and landslides.

Another $8 million will be directed towards water, sanitation and hygiene services, as well as shelter, protection and livelihood assistance.

Part of that allocation will support winterization programmes for communities facing colder weather without adequate housing or infrastructure.

The State Department said the new announcement would raise total US assistance for Nepal’s flood response and recovery to more than $36 million.

“The United States will continue to work closely with the Government of Nepal to identify and deliver additional assistance where it is most needed,” the department said.

September 22 meeting took place on the sidelines of high-level diplomatic engagements in New York, where world leaders and senior officials had gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.

US authorities are also working to locate American citizens caught in the affected areas. Earlier reports said some Americans had reached safety, but the new State Department statement said approximately 70 remained unaccounted for. (IANS)

A Georgia couple who narrowly escaped Nepal’s deadly August flooding recalled the precise moment that a last-minute decision took them out of the path of devastation.

Mita and Hemant Parikh, of Suwanee, were in the area after planning for 15 years to make a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in the Himalayas in Tibet, a sacred site in Hinduism.

“Everybody has a bucket list, but this bucket list, you don’t choose it,” Mita told CBS Atlanta. “God chooses for you.”

They were joined by 47 travelers including families from Australia, other parts of the US and elsewhere, with seven guides leading the group.

On impulse, the couple decided to take a side trip to view Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, which turned out to be a life-saving excursion.

title: “I’ve Never Feared Anything—but Avalanches.” Deadly Snowfall Has Climbers Fleeing a Himalayan Peak. - Outside Magazine
description: “I’ve Never Feared Anything—but Avalanches.” Deadly Snowfall Has Climbers Fleeing a Himalayan Peak.  Outside Magazine
publisher.title: Outside Magazine
full_article:
Updated September 23, 2026 03:59PM

Foul weather and deadly avalanches just spoiled the climbing season on one of Nepal’s most popular high peaks not named Mount Everest.

And with heavy snow in the forecast, it’s doubtful that any more climbers will make it to the top of 26,781-foot Manaslu before the season ends in October.

A Stepping Stone to Mount Everest

Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest peak, has in recent years become a popular destination for Everest hopefuls. The ascent takes in 8,000 vertical feet from Base Camp to the summit, and climbers must endure painfully thin air, ascents on glacier and rock, and time spent in the Death Zone. But the route does not feature the same sheer dropoffs or sections of technical climbing found on more challenging 8,000-meter peaks such as K2 or Annapurna.

View this post on Instagram

Most of Nepal’s largest commercial guiding outfitters offer Manaslu expeditions for the fall climbing season, which runs from late August until early October.

ADVERTISEMENT

“Manaslu is the most accessible 8000-meter peak in Nepal,” the American guiding company Summit Climb boasts on its website.

Still, the peak is no cakewalk. Base Camp is often battered by rain and sleet. Heavy snow regularly falls in the Himalayas in late summer and early fall, raising the potential for avalanches at higher elevation. In 2012, a massive slide roared down the peak and wiped out Camp III, leaving 11 climbers dead. In 2022, American extreme skier Hilaree Nelson was killed on Manaslu when an avalanche knocked her off a 5,000-foot slope.

“After climbing and skiing on some 40 of the world’s major 6,000-, 7,000-, and 8,000-meter peaks, this is the only mountain I could not recommend to anyone,” mountaineering expert and author Mike Marlot wrote in Outside in 2012. “It is avalanche central.”

Alas, the climbing world seems to have ignored Marlot’s sentiment, and in recent years scores of climbers have flocked to Manaslu, making it the second-most-popular 8000-meter peak in Nepal behind Everest.

ADVERTISEMENT

For 2026, Nepal’s Department of Tourism sold 493 climbing permits for Manaslu for the fall season, according to the Himalayan Times . For comparison, Nepal issued 494 climbing permits for Mount Everest this spring, the biggest year on record.

Heavy Snow and Deadly Slides

Expeditions began completing their acclimatization rounds on the peak in early September, and a team of rope fixers from the Expedition Operators Association of Nepal began laying fixed lines on the upper flanks of the peak during the second week of September. According to Everest Chronicle, the lines to the summit were completed on Thursday, September 17, three days ahead of the 2025 date.

Rope fixers encountered deep fresh snow and avalanches on the push to the summit. Then, storm clouds descended on the peak, dropping feet of new powder. The new snow raised the avalanche danger as climbers prepared to launch their bids for the summit.

Veteran guide Mingma G posted a video of an avalanche roaring down the flanks of Manaslu on September 16. The massive slide narrowly avoided taking out several tents at Camp III.

View this post on Instagram

“I have done every kind of climbing and never feared anything—but snow avalanches are the one thing that has always scared me,” Mingma G wrote on Instagram. “Yes, you can use some of your skills, but ultimately it all comes down to luck. Yesterday was a lucky day on Manaslu. Fortunately nobody was above Camp III.”

Climbers’ luck ran out several days later. On the night of September 20, an avalanche struck Camp III at 22,000 feet, killing two climbers as they were in their tent. The next day, crews found the bodies of German-Indian climber Dhrubajyoti Guha and guide Phursemba Sherpa, both 47, buried under several feet of snow.

ADVERTISEMENT

“Six other climbers who decided to retreat from Camp II are safe, but Guha and Sherpa decided to make an early summit attempt and headed for Camp III,” Mohan Lamsal, the managing director of guiding company Makalu Adventure told the Times of India. “ We sent four Sherpa climbers to Camp III to look for them. They dug through the snow and found both inside their tent, buried beneath nearly seven feet of snow.”

Makalu Adventure canceled its expedition after the fatalities, according to Everest Chronicle, and the surviving members of the ascent flew to lower elevations the day after the disaster.

The two fatalities raised the 2026 death toll on Manaslu to four: a climber from Singapore died on September 17 during his acclimatization ascent, and a Nepali porter was found dead in his tent in Base Camp earlier in the season.

Guides and Climbers Retreat as a Cyclone Bears Down

The heavy snow continued to batter climbers above Base Camp, and on September 1, climber Pastenji Sherpa from the guiding company Altipro Adventures posted a dramatic video of an avalanche engulfing Camp I at 18,700 feet.

“The mountain showed its true power,” Pastenji Sherpa wrote. “Moments like this remind us that in the high Himalayas, nature is always in control.”

View this post on Instagram

Mother Nature appeared unwilling to cut the Manaslu expeditions a break. With more heavy snowfall predicted for the peak, individual climbers and entire expeditions began heading for lower elevations on September 22.

ADVERTISEMENT

Veteran climber Simone Moro, who also flies rescue helicopters on Mount Everest and other peaks, abandoned his ascent after reaching Camp III that day. Moro wrote on Instagram that he then descended from Base Camp after he received a meteorological forecast that showed heavy snow headed for the peak from September 24 through the 28.

“At least two meters of fresh snow on any big mountain in Nepal from west to east,” Moro wrote. “The message was clear for those who want to listen, understand, and follow evidence.”

Others followed suit. Mingma G announced that his team was vacating Base Camp on September 23 as well. “Persistent snowfall created dangerous conditions, with risk of avalanches near Base Camp too,” he wrote. 8K Expeditions, another large guiding outfitter, told followers it was “pausing” its Manaslu expedition “until conditions improve.”

Seven Summits Treks, one of the largest outfitters, went further, saying that it was calling off its Manaslu expedition altogether.

With more snowfall predicted to fall on Manaslu in the coming days, the hopes of any climbers reaching the summit before the season closes in early October is slim. Those hoping to reach the top would likely need to dig out the now-buried fixed lines that rope fixers installed more than a week ago. In most years, expeditions wrap up their final summit pushes during the first week of October.

ADVERTISEMENT

Explorersweb, a mountaineering website, summed up the situation in a headline published on September 22: “Game Over on Manaslu.”

WASHINGTON (Diya TV) — The United States announced $31 million in additional aid Tuesday to help Nepal recover from the deadly Aug. 26 floods, bringing total U.S. assistance to more than $36 million.

The floods struck Nepal’s northern border region after a rock and ice collapse triggered a torrent of water, mud and debris. Nepalese authorities reported more than 1,400 deaths and more than 6,000 people missing in mid-September.

U.S. Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker announced the funding after meeting Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Hooker also expressed condolences to affected families, including those of approximately 70 Americans who remain unaccounted for.

The State Department plans to work with Congress to provide $10 million for permanent bridges built by a U.S. company. The bridges would restore transportation routes damaged by the floods.

Another $8 million will fund water and sanitation services, shelter, livelihood assistance, protection programs and winter supplies. The department also plans to provide $13 million in U.S.-made drones for disaster recovery operations.

The United States initially sent a disaster-response adviser and committed $500,000 in emergency assistance. It later expanded its response to include food, medical supplies, recovery equipment and forensic support for identifying victims.

U.S. Rep. Grace Meng, a New York Democrat whose district includes Nepali and Tibetan communities, had urged administration officials to increase the response. Meng said the new commitment marked an improvement but remained below the level of assistance affected communities need.

The State Department said it will continue working with Nepal’s government to identify additional recovery needs.

Scientists have discovered a new species of blind snake living among the forests of China’s Qinghai-Xizang Plateau – the world's largest and highest terrestrial plateau, with an area of 2,500,000 square kilometres (970,000 square miles).

The snake ( Indotyphlops gyirongensis ), described in the journal ZooKeys , was found on a roadside in a forest near the China-Nepal border.

The female specimen measured 26.5cm in length and had a light cream-coloured head cap and light brown body, gradually fading towards the tail.

Like all blind snakes – which either live underground or among logs and leaf litter – the individual had reduced eyes located under her head scales. The scientific name for blind snakes, Scolecophidia, derives from two Ancient Greek words, which translate as ‘earthworm’ and ‘snake’, in reference to their appearance and underground lifestyle.

Comparing its physical characteristics and DNA with other species of blind snake, the researchers determined that the new species belongs to a family of blind snakes known as Typhlopidae – the most species-rich and broadly distributed of the five families of blind snake.

“We suggest the English common name ‘Gyirong blind snake’ [referring to Gyirong Town, near where the snake was discovered] and the Chinese common name ‘吉隆盲蛇’ (Jílóng Mángshé) for this new species,” say the authors in the study.

Currently, the new species is known only from Xizang, China, but because the discovery was made so close to the China-Nepal border, the team thinks I. gyirongensis likely occurs in regions of Nepal.

“In recent years, with the extensive field exploration being conducted in Xizang, China, many new taxa or new national records have been recorded, particularly on the borders between China and its neighbours such as India, Nepal and Bhutan,” say the authors, “indicating these regions need further investigation.”

title: Nepal flood victims look to PM Shah to press climate case at UN - France 24
description: Nepal flood victims look to PM Shah to press climate case at UN  France 24
publisher.title: France 24
full_article:
Balendra Shah, 36, will press for international support at the UN General Assembly this week after the disaster that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing in Nepal and China's Tibet region.

Scientists say climate change played a key role in the August 26 floods, fuelling Nepal's argument that vulnerable mountain nations are paying a heavy price for a crisis they did little to create.

For teenager Karma Lama, that argument is rooted in his devastating loss.

The 17-year-old lost his parents and five other relatives when torrents of water, mud and debris swept through mountain communities.

"We need homes, we need a livelihood... big countries of the world should know our plight," the 17-year-old told AFP from a temporary shelter.

"He has to speak for us, for the flood victims."

Lama was on his way to school when the flood struck.

Flood victim Karan Tamang walks outside his tent at a temporary shelter area in Nepal's Nuwakot district © PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP

With roads and bridges washed away, he walked for hours through forests to reach his village in the badly hit Rasuwa district, only to find it gone.

"What I really want is my parents back. But that is not possible.

Almost a month after the catastrophe, helicopters still ferry food and medicine to isolated settlements while rescue teams continue searching for bodies.

Across Nepal's flood-hit valleys, thousands face the same uncertain future.

Rethinking projects

In Nuwakot district, excavators claw through debris through houses buried beneath mounds of grey silt.

Shoes and schoolbooks remain scattered across the ruins, with air conditioners hanging outside windows.

Flood victims Sobita Rijal and her husband Badri Prasad Rijal walk near their shop, damaged during the August 26 flash flood, at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district © PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP

Among those being forced to start over is Sobita Rijal, 35, who still has the keys to the three-storey home where she and her husband once ran a small shop.

Half the building now lies beneath debris, and the family now lives in a cramped rented room.

"I don't know what caused this, I don't know what climate change is," she said.

"But what I can say is that we need help... we are a small country."

The disaster has exposed the risks facing communities living below the world's highest peaks, where even a small increase in global temperatures can destabilise glaciers and river systems.

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people that contributes only a tiny share of greenhouse gas emissions, estimates reconstruction could cost $4.78 billion.

The country must not only rebuild towns and transport links, but also decide how to resettle thousands displaced by the flood.

It will also have to rethink infrastructure projects, including hydropower plants and trade corridors built in fragile mountain terrain.

'Pain is deep'

Scientists from the World Weather Attribution group have said climate change was a key driver of the disaster, describing it as a "compound crisis" fuelled by long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability rather than a single extreme weather event.

The flooding has added urgency to Nepal's calls for climate finance and compensation from wealthy nations.

Countries agreed to create a "loss and damage" fund in 2025 to help vulnerable states cope with climate impacts, although payments have yet to begin.

The stakes extend far beyond Nepal.

People look at damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal’s Nuwakot district © PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP

Glaciers across the wider Hindu Kush-Himalayan region supply water to some 240 million people in the mountains and another 1.65 billion living downstream across South and Southeast Asia.

Manjeet Dhakal of Climate Analytics said the disaster gave Nepal "a very strong ground" to make the case for climate justice before the international community.

"We should... remind the global community of its responsibility to urgently reduce emissions to limit temperature rise and scale up support for climate action in vulnerable countries," he said.

"This sympathy has to be translated into real action."

Survivors such as 51-year-old Narayan Prasad Khatiwada hopes that the suffering of those who lost everything is not forgotten once the world's attention moves on.

"We are a small country. If we had all the resources we would not need support from anyone. The big countries must help," he said.

"I hope the prime minister delivers a good message. Our pain is deep, very deep."
